title: Palitaw
intro: Flat glutinous rice cakes boiled until they float, then rolled in grated coconut and sprinkled with sugar and toasted sesame. Soft, chewy and mildly sweet.

steps.text: Mix the flour and water into a soft, smooth dough. Add water a spoonful at a time if it cracks.
Pinch off tablespoon-size pieces, roll into balls and flatten into ovals about 1/4 inch thick.
Bring a large pot of water to a boil and drop in a few pieces at a time. When they float, cook 1 minute more.
Lift out with a slotted spoon, shake off the water and roll in the grated coconut.
Mix the sugar and sesame seeds and sprinkle over the palitaw. Serve the same day.

tips: Do not crowd the pot or the cakes stick together. Fresh coconut spoils quickly at room temperature, so eat palitaw within the day or keep it chilled.

title: Ube palitaw
intro: Palitaw with ube halaya kneaded into the dough, so each chewy cake is purple and tastes of sweet yam. Rolled in coconut, sugar and sesame like the classic.

steps.text: Mix the ube halaya, ube extract and water, then work it into the flour to a soft, smooth dough that does not stick to your hands.
Pinch off tablespoon-size pieces, roll into balls and flatten into ovals about 1/4 inch thick.
Boil the pieces in batches in a large pot of water. When they float, cook 1 minute more.
Lift out, shake off the water and roll in grated coconut.
Sprinkle with the sugar and sesame seeds and serve the same day.

tips: Ube halaya makes the dough softer: add the water slowly and stop when the dough no longer sticks to your hands.

title: Biko
intro: Sticky rice simmered in coconut milk and brown sugar until thick and glossy, then topped with crunchy golden latik. Chewy, caramel sweet and made for sharing at parties.

steps.text: Make the latik: simmer the coconut cream, stirring more often as it thickens, until the oil separates and the curds are deep golden. Strain and keep the oil.
Cook the rice with the water in a rice cooker or covered pot until just tender.
In a wide pan, simmer the coconut milk, brown sugar and salt, stirring, until reduced by about a third and thick.
Add the rice and stir over low heat until the liquid is absorbed and the biko is very thick, sticky and pulls away from the pan.
Line a tray with banana leaves brushed with latik oil, spread the biko evenly and top with the latik. Cool before slicing.

tips: Cook the latik and rice at the same time to save time. Biko keeps 2 days covered at room temperature, longer in the fridge; warm it briefly before serving.

title: Biko with langka
intro: Biko cooked with strips of ripe jackfruit, so the sticky rice picks up the fruit's sweet, floral flavor. Topped with more jackfruit and toasted coconut.

items.name: grated coconut
items.note: toasted in a dry pan until golden

steps.text: Cook the rice with the water in a rice cooker or covered pot until just tender.
In a wide pan, simmer the coconut milk, brown sugar and salt, stirring, until reduced and thick.
Add the rice and half the jackfruit and stir over low heat until very thick and sticky.
Spread the biko on a tray lined with banana leaves and top with the remaining jackfruit and the toasted coconut.
Cool before slicing.

tips: Bottled jackfruit in syrup works: drain it and cut the brown sugar by 1/4 cup. Toast the coconut over low heat, stirring, so it browns evenly.

title: Ube biko
intro: Purple biko made with ube halaya stirred into the sticky rice, then topped with a layer of more halaya. Creamy, sweet and chewy, finished with latik or cheese.

steps.text: Cook the rice with the water in a rice cooker or covered pot until just tender.
In a wide pan, simmer the coconut milk, sugar, condensed milk, 1/2 cup of the ube halaya, the ube extract and salt, stirring, until smooth and slightly thick.
Add the rice and stir over low heat until very thick and sticky.
Spread on a tray lined with banana leaves and spread the remaining 1 cup ube halaya over the top in an even layer.
Sprinkle with latik or cheese and cool before slicing.

tips: Use white sugar here: brown sugar dulls the purple. Ube biko keeps 3 days in the fridge.

title: Pirurutong biko
intro: Biko made with pirurutong, a purple heirloom glutinous rice, which gives it a deep violet color and a nutty, slightly firmer chew. Finished with a baked muscovado and coconut topping.

steps.text: Drain the pirurutong and cook it with the white glutinous rice and water in a covered pot until tender.
In a wide pan, simmer the coconut milk, muscovado and salt, stirring, until reduced and thick.
Add the rice and stir over low heat until very thick and sticky.
Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Spread the biko in a 9 by 13-inch pan lined with banana leaves. Simmer the coconut cream and muscovado until thick, then spread it over the rice.
Bake until the topping bubbles and darkens.
Cool before slicing.

tips: Pirurutong is harder than white glutinous rice, so soak it at least 4 hours or overnight. Mixing it half and half with white glutinous rice keeps the biko sticky enough to slice.

title: Cassava cake
intro: Grated cassava baked with coconut milk, condensed milk and eggs into a dense, chewy cake, then topped with a creamy custard that browns under the broiler. One of the easiest kakanin for parties.

items.name: butter
items.note: melted, plus more for the pan

steps.text: Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) and butter a 9 by 13-inch pan.
Mix all the cake ingredients until evenly blended.
Pour into the pan and bake until set and firm in the center.
Whisk the condensed milk, coconut milk and egg yolks, pour over the cake and scatter the cheese on top. Bake until the topping is set.
Broil until spotted brown, watching closely.
Cool completely before slicing.

tips: If using fresh cassava, squeeze out some juice but not all; the cake needs moisture. Frozen grated cassava works well once fully thawed.

title: Cassava cake with macapuno
intro: Cassava cake studded with sweet macapuno strings, both in the cake and on top under the custard. The soft coconut strands add a chewy, syrupy sweetness.

items.name: butter
items.note: melted, plus more for the pan

steps.text: Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) and butter a 9 by 13-inch pan.
Mix all the cake ingredients with half the macapuno until evenly blended.
Pour into the pan and bake until set and firm in the center.
Whisk the condensed milk, coconut milk and egg yolks and pour over the cake. Scatter the remaining macapuno on top and bake until the topping is set.
Broil until spotted brown, watching closely.
Cool completely before slicing.

tips: Macapuno in syrup is sweet, so this version uses less sugar. Drain it well, or the cake turns soggy.

title: Pichi-pichi
intro: Soft, sticky, translucent cassava cakes steamed in small molds and rolled in freshly grated coconut. Chewy, gently sweet and best eaten the same day.

items.name: cassava
items.note: very finely grated (about 450 g), liquid squeezed out

steps.text: Mix the cassava, sugar and water until the sugar dissolves, then stir in the lye water and pandan flavoring.
Oil small puto molds or an 8-inch square pan, fill with the mixture and bring the steamer to a boil.
Steam until translucent all the way through, with no white spots.
Cool completely before unmolding or cutting.
Roll each piece in grated coconut.

tips: Pichi-pichi needs very finely grated cassava; coarse gratings stay stringy. Do not skip the cooling: warm pichi-pichi is too soft to roll.

title: Cheese pichi-pichi
intro: Pichi-pichi rolled in finely grated cheese instead of coconut, so each soft, chewy cassava bite is both sweet and salty. It also keeps longer than the coconut version.

items.name: cassava
items.note: very finely grated (about 450 g), liquid squeezed out

steps.text: Mix the cassava, sugar and water until the sugar dissolves, then stir in the lye water.
Oil small puto molds or an 8-inch square pan, fill with the mixture and bring the steamer to a boil.
Steam until translucent all the way through, with no white spots.
Cool completely before unmolding or cutting.
Roll each piece in the grated cheese, pressing lightly so it sticks.

tips: Grate the cheese on the finest holes and keep it cold so it coats evenly. Covered in the fridge, these keep 3 days.

title: Ube pichi-pichi
intro: Pichi-pichi flavored and colored with ube, steamed until translucent and rolled in grated coconut. The cassava stays soft and chewy, with a sweet purple yam flavor.

items.name: cassava
items.note: very finely grated (about 450 g), liquid squeezed out

steps.text: Whisk the ube halaya and ube extract into the water until smooth. Mix with the cassava and sugar until the sugar dissolves, then stir in the lye water.
Oil small puto molds or an 8-inch square pan, fill with the mixture and bring the steamer to a boil.
Steam until translucent all the way through, with no white spots.
Cool completely before unmolding or cutting.
Roll each piece in grated coconut.

tips: Mix the halaya into the water first so it spreads evenly. For a mixed tray, roll half in coconut and half in grated cheese.

title: Nilupak na kamoteng kahoy
intro: Boiled cassava pounded while hot with butter, sugar and grated coconut into a smooth, sticky mash, then shaped into rounds. Rich and buttery, it is eaten warm with more butter on top.

items.name: cassava
items.note: peeled, cored and cut into chunks

steps.text: Boil the cassava in salted water until very tender and starting to split.
Drain well. While still hot, pound in a large mortar or mash with a potato masher together with the sugar, condensed milk, butter and salt until smooth and sticky.
Fold in the grated coconut.
Press into oiled small molds or shape into rounds on a banana leaf.
Serve warm, topped with a little butter.

tips: Remove the woody core from each piece of cassava before boiling. Pound or mash while hot; cooled cassava turns lumpy.

title: Nilupak na saging
intro: Boiled saba bananas pounded with butter, sugar and grated coconut into a sweet, sticky mash and shaped into small rounds. Fruity, buttery and simple.

steps.text: Boil the bananas in their skins until tender.
Peel while hot and pound or mash with the brown sugar, butter and salt until smooth.
Fold in the grated coconut.
Shape into small rounds or press into a lined dish and slice.
Serve warm with a little butter on top.

tips: Use saba that is just ripe, yellow with a few black spots. Very ripe bananas make a wet mash that will not hold its shape.

title: Latik
intro: Crunchy golden curds made by slowly cooking coconut milk until the oil separates and the solids brown. Nutty and rich, latik is sprinkled on biko, kalamay and other kakanin.

steps.text: Pour the coconut milk into a wide pan, add the pandan leaf and bring to a boil over medium heat.
Lower the heat to medium-low and simmer, stirring now and then, until the water cooks off, the oil separates and white curds form.
Keep cooking, stirring more often, until the curds turn golden and then medium brown.
Strain through a sieve. Drain the curds on paper towels and keep the oil in a clean jar.
Sprinkle the latik on biko, kalamay, sapin-sapin or suman. Use the oil to grease pans and banana leaves.

tips: The curds go from golden to burnt in a minute near the end, so stay at the stove. The fragrant coconut oil keeps for weeks and is ideal for greasing kakanin pans.

title: Latik syrup
intro: A thick, glossy caramel of coconut milk and muscovado, simmered until it coats a spoon. It is the sauce for suman, puto maya and plain sticky rice.

steps.text: Combine the coconut milk, muscovado and salt in a saucepan and stir over medium heat until the sugar dissolves.
Simmer, stirring often, until reduced by about half, thick and glossy enough to coat a spoon.
Let it cool; it thickens more as it stands.

tips: If it turns too thick or grainy after cooling, warm it with a splash of coconut milk. It keeps 1 week in the fridge.

title: Homemade tikoy
intro: A dense, sticky brown sugar rice cake steamed in a round pan, the kind shared at Chinese New Year. Chewy and caramel sweet; eat it as is or slice and fry it once it firms up.

steps.text: Dissolve the brown sugar in the hot water and let it cool until warm.
Stir the syrup into the flour gradually and whisk to a smooth, thick batter like honey. Add the oil.
Oil a 7-inch round pan, line with banana leaf or baking paper and pour in the batter.
Steam over medium heat, topping up the water as needed, until the tikoy is evenly translucent brown with no white center.
Cool, cover and leave at room temperature overnight before slicing.

tips: Tikoy needs an overnight rest to firm up for slicing; it is too soft while warm. Wrapped well, it keeps 2 weeks in the fridge.

title: Fried tikoy with egg
intro: Slices of sweet sticky tikoy dipped in beaten egg and pan-fried until golden outside and gooey within. A quick, warm merienda.

steps.text: Chill the tikoy so it is firm, then cut into slices about 1/4 inch thick, wiping the knife with oil between cuts.
Beat the eggs with the salt in a shallow bowl.
Heat the oil in a nonstick pan over medium heat. Dip the slices in egg and fry in batches until golden and the centers are soft, about 2 minutes per side.
Drain briefly and serve hot.

tips: Keep the heat at medium: too hot and the egg browns before the tikoy softens. Leave space between slices so they do not stick together.

title: Moche
intro: Chewy glutinous rice balls filled with sweet mung bean paste, boiled and served with a thick, sweet coconut sauce and toasted sesame. Soft outside, smooth and nutty inside.

steps.text: Simmer the mung beans in the water until very soft and the water is absorbed.
Mash the beans, stir in the sugar and cook, stirring, until a thick paste that holds its shape. Let it cool.
Mix the flour and water into a smooth dough. Flatten a tablespoon of dough, put 1 tsp of filling in the center and seal into a ball.
Boil the balls in batches. Once they float, cook 2 minutes more, then lift out.
For the sauce, simmer the coconut milk and sugar, stir in the cornstarch mixture and cook until thick.
Serve the moche in small bowls with the sauce spooned over and sesame seeds sprinkled on top.

tips: Seal the balls well so the filling does not leak while boiling. Make the mung bean paste a day ahead to save time.

title: Masi
intro: Small glutinous rice balls with a filling of chopped peanuts and muscovado that melts into syrup as they boil. Chewy outside, crunchy and caramel sweet inside.

steps.text: Mix the chopped peanuts and muscovado.
Mix the flour and water into a soft, smooth dough.
Flatten a tablespoon of dough in your palm, add 1 tsp of filling and pinch closed. Roll into a smooth ball.
Boil the balls in batches. Once they float, cook 2 minutes more.
Lift out with a slotted spoon, drain and serve warm.

tips: Seal the balls well and do not overfill, or the melting sugar leaks into the water. Eat masi warm, while the center is still runny.

title: Baye-baye
intro: Toasted ground pinipig pounded with young coconut and sugar into a dense, chewy sweet. Nutty and coconut-rich, it is wrapped in banana leaves and sliced.

steps.text: Toast the pinipig in a dry pan over medium-low heat, stirring, until fragrant and golden.
Grind to a coarse powder in a blender.
In the same pan, cook the young coconut, coconut water, sugar and salt until the sugar dissolves and turns syrupy.
Off the heat, mix in the ground pinipig and knead or pound until it holds together as a stiff paste.
Shape into logs, wrap in banana leaves and let them rest before slicing.

tips: If the mixture is too dry to hold together, add coconut water a spoonful at a time. Eat within 2 days; keep chilled.
